A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Abstract Gradient Training (AGT) work. The complete main texts, equations, figures, table and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material from v1's Appendices A–D to v2's expanded appendices.

before.justification: Figures 1–5 report original certification experiments on halfmoons, household power consumption, OCTMNIST and autonomous driving.

after.justification: Original certification experiments remain, supplemented by MNIST results and empirical poisoning-attack experiments in Appendix H.

M1.justification: v2 extends AGT to unbounded sample substitutions through per-sample gradient clipping and a new descent-direction bound (Algorithm 1 and Appendix B). Clipping is optional for bounded attacks but required for the new unbounded case. The underlying interval/CROWN propagation framework remains.

E1.justification: v2 adds multiclass MNIST digit recognition under label flipping, extending the evaluated tasks beyond regression and binary classification. It also evaluates unbounded poisoning on OCTMNIST and targeted feature-collision poisoning on household data. The earlier datasets remain represented.

E2.justification: Appendix H introduces three empirical attack comparators: PGD-based parameter-targeted poisoning, randomized feature-collision poisoning and randomized label flipping. v1 had no corresponding attack-versus-certificate comparisons. The newly discussed partition/aggregation certification methods are cited, not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes OCTMNIST's learning rate from 0.005 to 0.05, decay from 10 to 5, and batch size from 10000 to 6000. The main text changes Drusen's batch share from 30% to 50%, although Appendix J retains the old mixture description. MNIST adds PCA to 32 dimensions, a linear classifier and a three-epoch, full-batch protocol.

E4.justification: The earlier adversary-strength and training-hyperparameter sweeps remain. v2 adds clipping sensitivity experiments and Appendix H's investigations of parameter-trajectory enclosure, targeted-loss bounds and accuracy under actual label poisoning. These directly examine certificate looseness and the utility–certification tradeoff.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The displayed certified intervals are worst-case guarantees, not statistical uncertainty estimates. v2's randomized attacks do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds MNIST, unbounded-poisoning and empirical-attack outcomes. Figure 4's accompanying text revises OCTMNIST's approximate feature/label poisoning thresholds from 90/120 to 500/at least 600 samples. These results use changed training settings and therefore do not establish a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: v2 adds an unbounded threat formalization, Theorem B.1 and its justification, computational-complexity analysis, and objective relaxations in Appendix G.2. It also corrects the CROWN upper-bound input coefficient from Omega to Lambda and the weight-gradient factor from current-layer preactivations to previous-layer activations. Much earlier mathematics is retained through relocation.

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly expands certification coverage to bounded and unbounded training-data manipulations. It also qualifies the novelty claim as providing guarantees without modifying the model or learning algorithm, sharpening the distinction from robust-learning defenses. The central parameter-space certification claim remains.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's depth and hyperparameter discussion, v2 explains the need for large batches or fewer epochs, weaker multiclass guarantees, clipping–utility tradeoffs and looseness relative to empirical attacks. These substantially clarify applicability limits. However, the prose incorrectly describes increasing the clipping threshold as improving guarantees; Figures 3–4 show the opposite trend at larger attack sizes.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the halfmoons model's 128-neuron hidden layer, MNIST preprocessing and training settings, and implementation recipes for the new attacks, including the feature-collision clipping threshold. These are localized reproducibility additions; the PyTorch implementation, hardware specification and repository access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The introduction and Appendix A add substantive positioning against partition/aggregation certification, including Levine and Feizi, Wang et al., and Rezaei et al. The discussion compares computational and data requirements, scalability and complementarity. Additional backdoor and unlearnable-example references broaden the positioning beyond merely relocating related work.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 2 to Appendix A, and the method exposition is extensively rewritten around descent-direction sets and a separate bounded-adversary theorem. Interval arithmetic, CROWN, gradient bounds and proofs are redistributed across appendices. Threat-model explanations and experimental narratives are also substantially revised.

P2.justification: The empirical figures are extensively reformatted. v1's Figures 2–3 become v2's combined Figure 2; MNIST receives Figure 3; Appendix H adds Figures 6–8. Figure 4 replaces its bounded joint-poisoning panel with an unbounded clipping comparison. Algorithm 1 is redesigned, and Table 1 gains a MNIST row.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidential gap by comparing certificates with actual poisoning attacks, exposing their looseness rather than presenting certification curves alone. MNIST results and explicit limitations substantially clarify applicability, while corrected bound-propagation expressions improve mathematical accuracy. Conflicting OCTMNIST mixture descriptions and reversed clipping-threshold prose remain reporting defects, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical assessment and clearer explanation of the guarantees' practical limits.
